questions.question: What do arrow functions NOT have of their own?

options.text: A return value
Their own 'this' binding (they inherit lexical this)
Parameters
A body

questions.explanation: Arrow functions capture 'this' from the enclosing scope — no own this, arguments, super, or new.target.

questions.question: Can you use `new` with an arrow function?

options.text: Yes, always
No — arrow functions are not constructors
Only if it has a body
Only in strict mode

questions.explanation: Arrows lack [[Construct]], so calling them with new throws a TypeError.

questions.question: Which arrow syntax implicitly returns a value (no 'return' keyword)?

options.text: const f = (x) => { x * 2 }
const f = x => x * 2
const f = (x) => { return; }
const f = function(x){ return x*2 }

questions.explanation: A concise-body arrow (no braces) implicitly returns its single expression.

questions.question: Inside an arrow function, what is `arguments`?

options.text: The arrow's own arguments array
The arguments of the enclosing (lexical) function, or undefined in module scope
Always an empty array
A SyntaxError

questions.explanation: Arrows have no own 'arguments'; they reference the outer function's arguments object.

questions.question: Why are arrow functions a poor choice for object methods that need `this`?

options.text: They are slower
They do not bind 'this' to the object, so 'this' is the enclosing scope
They cannot be named
They throw on call

questions.explanation: object.method = () => this.x uses lexical this (outer scope), not the method's receiver — typically unwanted.

questions.question: How do you return an object literal concisely with an arrow function?

options.text: () => return { foo: 1 }
() => new Object(1)

questions.explanation: Wrap the literal in parentheses so {} is parsed as an object, not a block body.
